name: Gotihawa
tagline: A broken Ashokan pillar tied to Krakuchchanda, a Buddha of the past
meta_description: Gotihawa in Kapilvastu: the stump of an Ashoka pillar and a brick stupa linked by tradition to Krakuchchanda Buddha. History, legend and how to visit.
summary: Gotihawa is a village in Kapilvastu district, a few kilometres south-west of Taulihawa, with the broken lower part of an Ashokan pillar and a brick stupa mound behind it. Buddhist tradition links it with Krakuchchanda, the first of the Buddhas of our age. Allow 30 minutes on a Kapilvastu day trip.
intro: At Gotihawa a stub of polished sandstone stands in a small fenced enclosure in the middle of the village, with a grassy brick mound behind it. It is the lower part of a pillar raised by Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE. The upper part, with any inscription it carried, is lost.

Buddhists know the place through an older story. Tradition says that long before Siddhartha Gautama, earlier Buddhas lived and taught in this same country. One of them, Krakuchchanda (Kakusandha in Pali), is said to have been born at Khemavati, which many identify with Gotihawa.

Most visitors come here as part of the Kapilvastu loop with Tilaurakot, Kudan and Niglihawa. It is a short stop, but standing next to an Ashokan pillar in a working village, with goats and children around you, is not something many places can offer.

story.title: The emperor who honoured Buddhas before the Buddha
paras: Buddhist texts teach that Siddhartha Gautama was not the first Buddha. The Buddhavamsa in the Pali Canon lists Buddhas of earlier ages, and names three who came before him in this one: Kakusandha, Konagamana and Kassapa. By the 3rd century BCE these earlier Buddhas had shrines in the Shakya country, and the emperor Ashoka honoured them as well as Gautama.

The Chinese pilgrims Faxian and Xuanzang, travelling south of Kapilavastu, described a stupa for Krakuchchanda Buddha with an Ashokan pillar beside it. When archaeologists followed their descriptions in the 19th and 20th centuries, Gotihawa, with its broken pillar and stupa mound, was the natural match.

In 1994–95 an Italian team led by Giovanni Verardi excavated at Gotihawa and studied the stupa and the pillar's setting. Some scholars think the inscribed pillar fragments at Niglihawa, a few kilometres away, may originally have stood on Gotihawa's base. Today the village grows rice, wheat and mustard right up to the fence, and the pillar is part of daily life.

legend: In the Buddhavamsa, Kakusandha Buddha was born to a brahmin family in the town of Khemavati, lived as a householder, left home after seeing the signs of age, sickness and death, and found enlightenment under a sirisa tree. Local tradition and many pilgrims place Khemavati at Gotihawa. The story mirrors Gautama's own life, which is the point the texts make: every Buddha walks the same road.
people: Gotihawa is a farming village of Awadhi-speaking Madhesi families, with Tharu and Muslim households in the surrounding settlements. People grow paddy in the monsoon and wheat, lentils and mustard in winter, and many families have members working in India or the Gulf. Children often gather around the pillar enclosure when visitors arrive, curious and happy to practise English.

untold.fact: In Theravada tradition Gotihawa was known in ancient times as Khemavati, birthplace of Kakusandha Buddha, whose life is told in chapter 22 of the Buddhavamsa in the Pali Canon.
An Italian archaeological mission led by Giovanni Verardi excavated at Gotihawa in the winter of 1994–95 and published its results in the journal Ancient Nepal in 1998.
untold.source: Wikipedia: Gotihawa; Ancient Nepal (Department of Archaeology), 1998

untold.fact: Scholars have suggested that the inscribed pillar fragments at Nigali Sagar, which were not found in their original place, may belong on the uninscribed pillar base at Gotihawa.

Mustard; the yellow winter crop in the fields around the pillar

taste.name: Sattu sharbat
taste.text: Roasted gram flour stirred into cold water with salt, lemon, cumin and sometimes green chilli: the plains drink for hot days. Small stalls in Taulihawa make it fresh from March onward. It is filling and cooling, and a good break between Gotihawa and Niglihawa.

highlights.title: The Ashokan pillar stump
highlights.text: The lower part of a polished sandstone pillar raised by Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE, still in place. The upper section and any inscription it carried are lost. The polish on the stone, typical of Mauryan work, is still visible.

highlights.title: The stupa mound
highlights.text: Behind the pillar is a brick stupa, excavated in the 1990s, which tradition links with Krakuchchanda Buddha. It is mostly a grassy mound today, with brickwork visible in places.

highlights.title: A pillar inside a village
highlights.text: Unlike Lumbini, Gotihawa has no garden or ticket office around it. Houses, haystacks and fields come right up to the enclosure, and you see the site as part of village life.

highlights.title: Mustard in bloom
highlights.text: In December and January the fields around Gotihawa turn yellow with mustard. Combined with the low winter sun, it makes this one of the most photogenic stops on the Kapilvastu loop.

highlights.title: The three earlier Buddhas
highlights.text: Gotihawa and Niglihawa are among very few places where Ashoka honoured the Buddhas before Gautama. A guide can explain the idea of past Buddhas and why it mattered to early Buddhists.

how_to_reach.text: Gotihawa is about 30 km west of Lumbini, roughly 1 hour by private car, and a few kilometres south-west of Taulihawa on village roads. Most visitors combine it with Tilaurakot, Kudan and Niglihawa in one day from Lumbini.
Fly Kathmandu to Bhairahawa, about 35 minutes, then drive about 50 km west to Gotihawa, around 1.5 hours.

where_to_stay: There are no hotels in Gotihawa. Stay in Lumbini, about an hour east, where Buddha Maya Gardens and the Lumbini Hokke Hotel are comfortable bases for the Kapilvastu sites. Taulihawa, a few kilometres north-east, has basic local hotels for anyone who wants to stay closer, with simple rooms and Nepali and Indian food.
tips: Do not climb on the stupa mound or touch the pillar's polished surface; both are protected monuments.
Ask before photographing villagers, especially women working in the fields.
There are no facilities at the site, so carry water and use toilets in Taulihawa.
Visit Gotihawa and Niglihawa together to compare the two Ashokan pillars for past Buddhas.
Mid-December to mid-January brings mustard in flower and the best winter light, though mornings may be foggy.

experiences.title: Ashoka's pillar in the middle of a village
experiences.summary: A short guided stop at the stump of Gotihawa's Ashokan pillar and the stupa mound behind it, with the story of Krakuchchanda Buddha and the archaeology that tied this village to the pilgrims' accounts.
body: We pull up at the edge of the village and walk the last few metres to the enclosure. Your guide starts with the stone itself: sandstone, worked and polished in the Mauryan style, set in the ground more than 2,200 years ago and broken at some point since.

Behind it the stupa mound rises a few metres above the fields. Your guide will explain what the Italian excavations of the 1990s found and how Faxian's and Xuanzang's descriptions of a stupa for Krakuchchanda Buddha led archaeologists here.

Then there is the bigger idea: that Ashoka, the greatest patron of early Buddhism, honoured not only Gautama but the Buddhas before him. The stump at Gotihawa is one of the few physical traces of that belief.

faqs.q: Does the Gotihawa pillar have an inscription?
faqs.a: No inscription survives on the Gotihawa pillar. Only the broken lower part remains in place, and the upper part, which may have carried an inscription and a capital, is lost. Some scholars think the inscribed fragments at Niglihawa may originally have belonged to this base.

faqs.q: Who was Krakuchchanda Buddha?
faqs.a: Krakuchchanda, called Kakusandha in Pali, is named in Buddhist texts as the first of the Buddhas of the present age, before Konagamana, Kassapa and Gautama. The Buddhavamsa says he was born at Khemavati, which tradition identifies with Gotihawa. Theravada Buddhists in particular honour these earlier Buddhas.

faqs.q: How long do I need at Gotihawa?
faqs.a: Thirty to 45 minutes is enough to see the pillar and stupa and hear the story. Gotihawa is usually combined with Tilaurakot, Kudan and Niglihawa in a 6–7 hour day trip from Lumbini, with lunch in Taulihawa.

experiences.title: Pilgrimage to the Buddhas of the past
experiences.summary: A half-day pilgrimage linking Gotihawa and Niglihawa, the two sites Ashoka marked for the earlier Buddhas Krakuchchanda and Kanakamuni, with readings from the Buddhavamsa and time to chant at each.
body: Most pilgrims to Lumbini follow Gautama's life. This half day follows a different thread: the Buddhas who came before him. At Gotihawa, linked to Krakuchchanda, and at Niglihawa, linked to Kanakamuni, Ashoka left pillars to honour them.

Your guide brings short readings from the Buddhavamsa for each Buddha: where they were born, under which tree they found awakening, and how their lives mirror Gautama's. At each site there is time to circle the stupa or pillar and chant or sit quietly.
The two sites are a short drive apart. The half day can be joined to Tilaurakot and Kudan for a full Kapilvastu circuit, or done alone from Lumbini.

faqs.q: Which past Buddhas are linked to the Kapilvastu sites?
faqs.a: Tradition links Gotihawa with Krakuchchanda (Kakusandha) Buddha and Niglihawa with Kanakamuni (Konagamana) Buddha, the first two of the three Buddhas before Gautama in the present age. Ashoka's inscription at Niglihawa names Konakamana directly, which is why that link is the stronger of the two.

faqs.q: Can non-Buddhists join this pilgrimage?
faqs.a: Yes. The half day suits anyone interested in Buddhist ideas or early Indian history. You are welcome to take part in chanting or simply listen. Dress modestly, walk clockwise around stupas and pillars, and do not climb on the monuments.

faqs.q: Do we need a Buddhist monk to lead the pilgrimage?
faqs.a: No. Our guide leads the visit and readings. If you would like a monk to join for chanting, we can ask at one of the Lumbini monasteries in advance; this depends on their schedule and a donation is customary. Let us know when you book.

experiences.title: Walk through the winter mustard fields
experiences.summary: A gentle hour on the field bunds around Gotihawa in December and January, when mustard flowers turn the plain yellow, with farmers at work, birds in the stubble and the pillar on the horizon.
body: In the Terai winter, after the rice harvest, many families sow mustard for oil. By late December the fields around Gotihawa are a sheet of yellow, broken only by mango trees, haystacks and the low mound of the stupa.

We walk the narrow earth bunds between fields with a local guide, stopping to talk with farmers where they are happy to chat. You will see the wheat coming up green, small irrigation channels and the clay-walled houses where families dry chillies and dung cakes in the sun.
The walk is flat and about 3 km. Late afternoon light is warm and low, which is what photographers come for.

faqs.q: When does mustard flower in the Nepal Terai?
faqs.a: Mustard is usually sown after the rice harvest in October and November and flowers from late December into January, depending on sowing time and weather. By February most fields are setting seed. For the brightest yellow, plan your Kapilvastu day for the last week of December or the first half of January.

faqs.q: Is it OK to walk through farmers' fields?
faqs.a: Walk only on the earth bunds and paths between fields, never through standing crops. Our guide asks permission where needed. Farmers in Kapilvastu are generally welcoming, but keep groups small and quiet, and ask before taking close photographs of people.

faqs.q: What should I wear for the field walk?
faqs.a: Wear closed shoes that can get dusty or muddy, light long trousers and a warm layer, as late afternoons in December and January cool quickly to around 12–15 °C. A hat and sunglasses help with the low sun. Modest clothing is appreciated in the villages.

experiences.title: Ashoka's pillar trail in one day
experiences.summary: A full day from Lumbini to see all three Ashokan pillars in Nepal: the inscribed pillar at Lumbini, the inscribed fragments at Niglihawa and the stump at Gotihawa, with Tilaurakot and Kudan on the way.
body: Nepal holds three of Ashoka's pillars, all within about 30 km of each other. This day sees them in order. We start at dawn at Lumbini, where the pillar carries the inscription naming the Buddha's birthplace, and read the Brahmi line together.

Then we drive west to Niglihawa, where two pillar fragments lie beside a pond, one with an inscription recording that Ashoka enlarged the stupa of Konakamana Buddha. From there it is a short drive to Tilaurakot for the walls of Kapilavastu, and lunch in Taulihawa.
In the afternoon we see Kudan's stupas and finish at Gotihawa, where the broken pillar still stands in its base. By sunset we are back in Lumbini, about 70 km of driving in all.

faqs.q: How many Ashoka pillars are there in Nepal?
faqs.a: There are three Ashokan pillar sites in Nepal, all in the Lumbini area: the inscribed pillar at Lumbini, the inscribed fragments at Niglihawa (Nigali Sagar) and the uninscribed stump at Gotihawa. Others survive in India, such as Rampurva and Lauriya Nandangarh in the West Champaran district of Bihar.

faqs.q: How much driving is the Ashoka pillar day?
faqs.a: About 70 km in total on flat roads, broken into short drives of 15–60 minutes between sites. The full day runs about 8–9 hours including stops and lunch. We use a private car with a driver who knows the village roads around Taulihawa.

faqs.q: Can I read the Ashoka inscriptions myself?
faqs.a: The Lumbini inscription is behind a railing but legible, and your guide carries a transliteration and translation to follow letter by letter. The Niglihawa inscription is on a fragment lying on the ground and is harder to see. Brahmi is not hard to learn at a basic level, and the guide will show you how.

faqs.q: Where is Gotihawa?
faqs.a: Gotihawa is a village in Kapilvastu district, Lumbini Province, a few kilometres south-west of Taulihawa and about 30 km west of Lumbini by road. It is roughly an hour's drive from Lumbini and is usually visited with Tilaurakot, Kudan and Niglihawa.

faqs.q: What is Gotihawa famous for?
faqs.a: Gotihawa is known for the broken lower part of an Ashokan pillar from the 3rd century BCE and a brick stupa behind it. Buddhist tradition links the site with Krakuchchanda, a Buddha who lived long before Gautama, said to have been born at Khemavati.

faqs.q: Is the Gotihawa pillar authentic?
faqs.a: Yes. The stump is accepted as part of a genuine Mauryan pillar of Ashoka's time, made of polished sandstone like the Lumbini pillar. What is uncertain is what its lost upper part said, and whether the inscribed fragments at Niglihawa came from it.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee at Gotihawa?
faqs.a: There has generally been no formal ticket office at Gotihawa; the pillar stands in a small enclosure in the village. Arrangements at the Kapilvastu sites are managed by the Lumbini Development Trust and Department of Archaeology and may change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do I get to Gotihawa from Lumbini?
faqs.a: Hire a private car or taxi from Lumbini; the drive is about 30 km and takes about an hour on village roads. Public transport is limited to buses to Taulihawa and e-rickshaws from there, so a car is far easier, especially if you are combining several sites.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Gotihawa?
faqs.a: October to March gives comfortable temperatures of 20–28 °C. Late December and January add yellow mustard fields but often morning fog. From April to June the heat passes 38 °C, and July to September brings monsoon rain and muddy village lanes.

faqs.q: Is Gotihawa worth visiting?
faqs.a: For pilgrims and anyone interested in Ashoka or early Buddhism, yes: it is one of only three Ashokan pillar sites in Nepal and a rare link to the idea of past Buddhas. It is a short stop, best combined with Tilaurakot, Kudan and Niglihawa rather than visited alone.

faqs.q: Who excavated Gotihawa?
faqs.a: Gotihawa was excavated in the winter of 1994–95 by an Italian archaeological mission led by Giovanni Verardi, working with Nepal's Department of Archaeology. Their results were published in the journal Ancient Nepal in 1998. Earlier surveys followed the accounts of Faxian and Xuanzang to the site.

faqs.q: Are there facilities at Gotihawa?
faqs.a: No. Gotihawa is a village site without toilets, cafes or shops for visitors beyond small local stores. Carry water, plan toilet stops at Tilaurakot or Taulihawa, and bring sun protection. Your driver will know where to park near the enclosure.
